title: Replicating carbonaceous vug in synthetic porous media
author: Khan, DiCarlo, et al.

steps.title: CT scan dolomite sample
steps.instruction: Scan the Guelph dolomite sample (38 mm × 72 mm, 3 mm thick) using the Universal Systems HD‑350E medical CT scanner at UT PGE with a voxel resolution of 250 µm.

steps.title: Extract vug surface in ImageJ
steps.instruction: Process the CT image stack in Fiji‑ImageJ: run the built‑in ‘find connected region’ algorithm to identify all 3D connected spaces, color‑code and isolate each region, select the desired vug, visualize it in the 3D viewer, and export the vug surface as an STL file.

substeps.instruction: Run ‘find connected region’ on the 3D image stack.
Color‑code and isolate individual connected spaces.
Visualize the selected vug in the built‑in 3D viewer.
Export the vug surface to STL format.

steps.title: 3D‑print vug model
steps.instruction: Load the exported STL into a MakerBot® Replicator 2 (located at UT PGE) and print the vug model using the printer’s standard settings.

steps.title: Create gypsum cement mold
steps.instruction: Create a mold around the 3D‑printed vug and cast the mold with gypsum cement to form a negative replica of the vug.

substeps.instruction: Prepare a mold that conforms to the printed vug geometry.
Mix gypsum cement according to manufacturer instructions.
Pour the gypsum into the mold and allow it to set.

steps.title: Sinter core with vug
steps.instruction: Place the gypsum‑cast vug into the dolomite core and sinter the assembly so that the vug remains in place within the synthetic porous media.

steps.title: Acid removal of gypsum
steps.instruction: Treat the sintered core with acid to dissolve and remove the gypsum cement, leaving the replicated vug intact.

steps.title: Validate vug via repeat CT scan
steps.instruction: Rescan the treated core in the same medical CT scanner, reconstruct the vug space using Fiji‑ImageJ, and compare the new visualization with the original to assess repeatability.

substeps.instruction: Scan the core using the HD‑350E scanner at the same settings.
Reconstruct the vug volume in Fiji‑ImageJ.
Overlay or compare the new vug visualization with the original STL‑based model.

description: A Guelph dolomite sample (38 mm × 72 mm) is scanned at a resolution of 250 μm [5] and thickness of 3 mm in a medical CT scanner (Universal Systems HD-350E located at UT PGE). The images are processed to isolate a vug and surface extracted. MakerBot® Replicator 2 (located at UT PGE) is used to 3D–print the surface. Mold is created and cast in gypsum cement (Fig. 1). Core is sintered with the casted vug in place and treated with acid to remove the gypsum cement.Fig. 1Surface visualization (left), resultant 3D–print (middle) and vug cast (right).Fig. 1 Core is scanned in the medical CT scanner and vug space is reconstructed using Fiji-ImageJ (Fig. 2). The vug visualizations are compared to validate the repeatability of the system.Fig. 2Vug space after acid flood.Fig. 2 The extremities are not captured well in the reconstruction, but this can be attributed to the limited resolution of the 3D–printed vug space.
